title: Hello, I'm Kendall.
text:
>>> kendall.hello_world()
      Hello, I'm Kendall.
    

    I'm a Statistics & Data Science graduate from UCLA with a Mathematics minor, originally from San Francisco and now based in Chicago. Today, I'm a Solutions Specialist at Databricks. I love to build, and I treat every project as a chance to push myself creatively and learn something new.

    Mostly in SQL Python R, always reproducible. Take a look at my work, read a bit about me, see the tools I work with, or get in touch.

          An end-to-end app I built to teach myself the Databricks platform. It runs on 50,000 synthetic players and 2M matches generated with dbldatagen, and it finds who's about to quit, what they're worth, and what catching them is worth to the business.
        
      
      
        
        
          Internship · Databricks · Summer 2026

          Shipped five Databricks Apps for partner and sales teams, from inbox analytics to a self-improving FAQ bot to a partner EBC hub.

          Cleaned and geocoded thousands of Savills lease records to find where post-pandemic office demand actually went. One of 70+ teams.

          Power-model fitting, quarter-over-quarter change detection, and climate-controlled unit comparisons across TX, CO, UT and CA.
        
      
      
        
        
          Capstone · Stats 140XP
          Does Party Control Change Drone Strike Lethality?
          Twenty years of Guardian records tested with Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney. Lethality differed significantly. Accuracy didn't.
        
      
    
  



  
    About
    These are just some of the projects I've worked on, but they say a lot about how I like to work. I'm drawn to data because there's always something deeper than the surface level, and I love digging in until it finally makes sense. Building is my favorite way to learn, so I'm usually in the middle of something new and figuring it out as I go.
    Outside of work, you'll find me exploring Chicago's restaurants, hanging out with my cat, or at a mahjong table. If something here caught your eye, I'd love to chat.

title: Projects.
text:
>>> kendall.projects()
      Projects.
    

    Projects that pushed me in different directions — a passion project I built to learn the Databricks platform, five production apps shipped during my Databricks internship, speed and collaboration under a 48-hour clock, business decision support with real money attached, and careful statistical inference on messy public data.

    
  



  

    
      
        
          
        
      
      The Player Intelligence Platform
      
        Passion project · Databricks App
        Databricks Apps
        Unity Catalog
        SQL Warehouse
        dbldatagen
        SQL
        Python
      
      I built this to teach myself the Databricks platform by taking everything I like about Databricks and pointing it at something I love outside of work: gaming. It's an end-to-end demo built around a fictional live-service battle-royale game at realistic scale. The 50,000-player sample stands in for a title with 400M+ accounts, with 2M matches played in a week.
      On the surface everything looks healthy: revenue is up and players are spending. Underneath, the game is quietly losing its most valuable players. There's no cancellation event and no warning; they just stop. The app walks through five chapters: find the players about to leave, prove what they're worth, and show what catching them is worth to the business.
      
        Generated all of the data synthetically with dbldatagen, with free-to-play spending patterns calibrated to published industry survey data
        Modeled four linked tables (players, matches, purchases, and match stats with MMR and rank) and governed them in Unity Catalog
        Served the front end as a Databricks App, with every figure queried live from a SQL Warehouse
        Surfaced the ~7.9K players who have stopped playing and may leave for good
        Added "choose your character" views that tailor the story for a LiveOps analyst, economy designer, data engineer, or finance lead
      
      Tools I used: Databricks Apps · Unity Catalog · Databricks SQL Warehouse · dbldatagen · SQL · Python
      Recording of the platform above — press play for a walkthrough.
    

    
      
        
          
        
      
      A Summer of Building: Five Production Databricks Apps
      
        Partner Sales Intern · Databricks · Summer 2026
        Databricks Apps
        FastAPI
        Gmail API
        Google Sheets
        HTML/CSS
      
      I spent summer 2026 on Databricks' Partner Strategy & Ops team as a Partner Sales intern. Over the summer I built, deployed, and iterated on five Databricks Apps that gave partner and sales teams visibility they didn't have before — each one designed hand-in-hand with the people who'd actually use it.
      
        Partner EBC Kit — a partner-facing hub for running Executive Briefing Centers: approved decks, live demos from the Partner Demo Catalog, build-your-own guides, and feedback surveys. Reframed the program from "how to run an EBC" to "how to feature Databricks in one."
        Partner FAQ Gap Console — a FAQ chatbot paired with a "Logged Gaps" console: every question the bot can't answer is routed to an SME, and the answer is fed back into the corpus so it doesn't fail the same way twice.
        Partner Inbox Discovery Dashboard — email volume, top senders, themes, and SLA across three partner inboxes, auto-refreshed from Gmail every 15 minutes.
        Partner Ops Inbox Dashboard — request-type routing across 13 categories, per-person assignment and reassignment, and full assignment history for the partner-ops and DCIF queues.
        PayG SDR Outreach Dashboard — pipeline visibility for 5 SDRs across 138 pay-as-you-go accounts, synced live from a Google Sheet.
      
      What I took from it: I came in technical and spent the summer growing the business side — sales instinct and strategy. The best tools came from shipping on real feedback, often turning a partner's feature request into a live change the same week.
      Recording of my internship readout above — press play for a walkthrough.
    

    
      
        
      
      Pinning Properties: LA Office Micro-Trends
      
        Team member · DataFest 2025
        R
        Python
        tidyverse
        ggplot2
        sqldf
        Geocoding
        Spatial viz
      
      UCLA's DataFest gives you a commercial dataset and 48 hours. Ours came from Savills: a large national record of U.S. office leasing. My team — the Dangerous Ducklings — set out to find where office demand actually went after the pandemic, rather than just confirming that it fell.
      We narrowed to Los Angeles County so we could say something specific instead of something vague. That meant cleaning and merging thousands of lease records, geocoding building addresses, and mapping how A-class and O-class buildings diverged block by block.
      
        Cleaned and merged high-volume leasing records across inconsistent address formats
        Geocoded buildings and mapped leasing activity spatially
        Built a scoring system to rank micro-markets by demand shift
        Delivered a presentation judged against 70+ competing teams
      
      What I took from it: scope discipline. The teams that tried to cover the whole country had nothing concrete to show at hour 48. Narrowing to one county was what made our findings legible.
      
        View the slides
      
    

    
      Power Pricing & Yearly Rent Dynamics
      
        Data Science Intern · Storage Star · Summer 2025
        SQL
        R
        tidyverse
        Power models
        Diagnostics
        Quarto
      
      During my summer internship at Storage Star, a self-storage operator, I built a multi-part analytics report on rent per square foot across their Texas, Colorado, Utah, and California markets. The question behind it was practical: where is pricing drifting, and is that drift real or noise?
      
        Quarter-over-quarter change detection across markets
        Power model fitting, with residual and diagnostic checks
        Climate-controlled vs. non-climate-controlled unit comparisons
        Outlier identification and sensitivity analysis to test how fragile each conclusion was
        Reproducible visualizations and reporting built in R and Quarto
      
      What I took from it: a model is only useful if someone can act on it. The sensitivity analysis mattered more to the people reading my report than the fitted coefficients did.
      The deliverable contains Storage Star's proprietary pricing data, so it isn't published here. Happy to walk through the methodology and findings in conversation.
    

    
      
        
      
      Does Party Control Change Drone Strike Lethality?
      
        Statistical Analyst · Stats 140XP Capstone
        R
        Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney
        Shapiro-Wilk
        Levene's test
      
      For our capstone, my group asked whether U.S. political party control is associated with the lethality, accuracy, and magnitude of drone strikes in Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia — using two decades of records compiled by The Guardian.
      The data was annual, non-normal, and unbalanced across administrations, so parametric tests were off the table. We built a cleaned yearly dataset, derived comparable metrics, and used nonparametric methods throughout.
      
        Transformed The Guardian's raw strike records into a clean annual dataset
        Derived comparable metrics including median people killed and accuracy ratios
        Tested partisan differences with Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney, validating assumptions with Shapiro-Wilk and Levene's
        Examined whether the 2012 "Near Certainty" policy changed outcomes
      
      Findings: lethality was significantly higher under Democratic presidents, while accuracy showed no significant difference. Strikes after the 2012 policy were significantly less lethal and more accurate. Because the data is observational, we framed all of this as association rather than cause.
